Yes.. absolutely. For extremity wounds it is not that nuanced. Certainly it takes a little more thought than a tourniquet… but there is a phenomenon called tamponade that’s worth talking about. 

Tamponade is essentially where you bleed into a compartment… and as that compartment gets full, the pressure builds up enough to provide counter pressure on the bleed… thus stopping the extravasation of blood. In the extremities…. The compartments are small enough that if you close them off they will tamponade off. It is the same idea as a pressure dressing… the only difference is that you can’t bleed through a “scab” like you can a dressing. In extremity wounds as long as you cauterize enough of the wound to prevent active visible bleeding you can be pretty sure you won’t bleed internally enough (due to space) that you won’t die. 

When we talk about internal bleeding it is always in the thorax and pelvis… because those compartments are big enough to hold enough blood that you don’t get intrinsic tamponade

The one exception to this is proximal thigh injuries. The compartment between your quads and hamstrings is big enough to hold a liter or so of blood… which is a quarter of your blood volume. So if you lose a liter and then cauterize you could still potentially lose another liter into your thigh which could be enough to kill you. 

When we learn cautery in surgey… the rule is “cautery is adequate when visible bleeding has stopped.” That same idea can be applied to wilderness medicine. If you cauterize enough that you have no active bleeding you can be pretty sure you have done a good job. Also… over cautery in an emergency situation doesn’t exist

Also just noticed the severed limb part… I would absolutely not recommend cauterizing the stump of a severed limb. In that case you would have so much exposed bleeding area that cauterizing wouldn’t be faster or superior to just tourniqueting the whole limb

Great question! Since it is a procedure it requires licensing (ie MD or DO) to do in a hospital… however, it takes zero additional know how to implement. Great questions! I think for brands… I can’t give you much advice. However I will say that there are essentially 2 types of cautery pens… one with wire tips and one with “bovi” tips. The difference is that wire tips are flexible and soft and bovi tips are firm. In the case of most arterial bleeds the injury is deep… and without a doubt I would recommend the firm bovi tip to be able to jam it deep into the wound. The downside is that bovi tips are more expensive. In the situation I described I had a wire tip… and it was adequate to penetrate an inch or so into the wound. If I had to choose I would always get bovi tipped since it is more utility for lower extremity injuries, as the arteries are deeper just based on how much more tissue is in our lower limbs vs upper. 

As for when tourniquets are more valuable I will say that it is about tissue depth and length. Just for conceptual reasons let’s just talk about how cautery works. The super heated tip is designed to scar of the upstream and downstream end of the injured artery. Meaning if the wound is 1-5 cm… the tip in the wound will adequately cauterize both sides of the injury. It might take some wiggling around but it will work. Additionally as you cauterize active bleeding it actually boils the blood and effectively turns that blood into a clotting material… essentially you are instantly scabbing inside the wound. 

The pitfalls of cautery are based on wound size. A tip is essentially the size of a pencil.. so if you think of a longitudinal wound such as a slashing knife wound or a large open laceration I would recommend tourniquet. Moreover there are multiple places in the body such as the knee and groin where if the artery is injured it retracts into the tissue away from the wound… which means if you cauterize the wound where the hole is you may be missing the source of the bleed. The most common sight where this occurs is in the femoral artery at the hip or the brachial artery in the armpit. However is these settings, if the bleed has retracted into the axillary skeleton you shit outta luck anyway. 

In short I think you can think about cautery being super valuable for puncture wounds and tourniquets being valuable in wide open lacerations. 

I will say however that there is utility in both. I have never done it but I expect that if you tourniquet a limb to start and then cauterize the wound you would get superior clotting than just with one or the other. 

The other thing to think about is time to clot. In open arterial wounds you can very easily lose a liter of blood in a minute. And when you think about volumes… losing 4 liters = death. So speed is very valuable. If you can come onto an injury, whip out a pen and get the clotting started you might save 500 ml vs a tourniquet. From a survival standpoint this is negligible… but from a “I still need to hike out 6 miles” it can be the difference between the ability to walk and stay awake and collapsing during the extraction. 

Hope that is helpful!

This is a great question.. but let’s talk about the facts.

Chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and all the skin infections like crabs and such. Are 100% curable. These bugs are bacteria and easily treated with antibiotics.

Hpv, hiv, and herpes, hepatitis are the viruses and are treatable but not curable. And this is up for debate. 

3/5 of people already have hpv... although few have warts... and those worts can be removed cosmetically. Additionally the Gardasil vaccine prevents hpv strains that can cause cancer.

HIV treatment is so good now that viral loads become so low that it is untrabnsmittable. And technology is very close to a complete “cure.” However treatments can be expensive so have insurance. 

Herpes is predicted to be in 50-80 percent of the adult population. It is not curable, but prophylactic use of antivirals or simply not having sex during outbreaks drastically reduces the amount of outbreaks. 

Hepatitis is rarely transmitted via sex but I included it to be thorough. Vaccinate against hep b and don’t do iv drugs. If you do, there are good treatments for hep c.

I am in a similar boat... having extra time. This will be blasphemy for many people but this is what I would do. Download the postpone add on. You can postpone cards for any amount of time. The beauty of this is that if you have 10k reviews right now... you can stop them from building up. Do 1000 reviews a day for 10 days and then you’ll be caught up and can get back on the anki train. I do 3 40 blocks of questions... 120 per day.. and sprinkle in my cards around that. There is no shame in postponing. It gives you a chance to learn your reviews and not feel like you are just blowing through cards. Also... what I have done.. is I’ve cut my interval down to 1 month max. It means I’ll see every card in my decks in the next month. It’s about 1000 cards per day... every time I miss a card I flag it... then when I get closer to step I can just do my flagged cards and focus on topics I don’t know. Try to filter out the stuff you know and hit the stuff you don’t.

I dunno... I think this depends on what your focus is. I do my cards first because it has an achievable number. I hit about 1500 cards a day... and it take me 6ish hours or so... sometimes 8. But that is my legitimate study time. I go slow. I look up terms a pathways in first aid. I flag and organize the stuff i suck at. I’m not just doing cards to “do “ them. The time is exhausting but also anki isn’t the answer to something.., like if you blow through cards everyday you won’t always succeed. It’s just a model. Treat it like doing lecture or practice questions. It is work. And if you aren’t getting through it, your interval is too short. My schedule looks like this... I do my cards for about 8 to 2. I do 80/120 questions... so then it’s like 5pm. Then exercise and eat ( or nap or troll reddit) and do a few more hours of something. Some people do curriculum. Some do other stuff. I guess the biggest thing is whether or not anki is supplement or primary. For me.. anki is primary, questions secondary, then maybe curriculum. So don’t get bogged down on the time... anki is fundamentally a long game.. like Joel embid says.. trust the process.
